Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates — types, sources, functions, daily requirement and role in health.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Classify carbohydrates with examples
  • State the functions of carbohydrates
  • Describe the role of fibre

In simple words

Carbohydrates are the body’s cheapest and main source of energy. One gram gives about 4 kilocalories (kcal). They are found mainly in plant foods — cereals, roots, fruits and sugar.

Carbohydrates are classified by size: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides. Complex carbohydrates (starch, fibre) are healthier than refined sugar.

Classification

Type Examples Food sources
Monosaccharides Glucose, fructose, galactose Fruits, honey
Disaccharides Sucrose, lactose, maltose Sugar, milk, malt
Polysaccharides Starch, glycogen, cellulose Rice, wheat, potatoes, vegetables

Functions

  • Main source of energy for the body and brain.
  • Spares protein so protein can be used for growth and repair.
  • Fibre (a polysaccharide) helps bowel movement and prevents constipation.
  • Helps store energy as glycogen in liver and muscle.

Daily requirement

About 50–60% of total daily energy should come from carbohydrates, mostly complex carbohydrates, not refined sugar.

🔴 Energy value

One gram of carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal. Carbohydrates should provide about 50–60% of daily energy, mostly from complex carbohydrates.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Diabetic diet — advise consistent carbohydrate intake; prefer complex carbs over sugar.
  • Energy needs — ensure sick patients get enough carbohydrates to spare protein for healing.
  • Constipation — encourage fibre-rich foods (whole grains, vegetables, fruits) and fluids.
  • Weight management — excess refined sugar and starch leads to weight gain.
  • Patient teaching — explain the difference between healthy carbs (whole grains) and unhealthy carbs (sweets, soft drinks).

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Carbohydrates are the body’s main and cheapest energy source.
  2. 1 g carbohydrate = about 4 kcal.
  3. Types: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides.
  4. 50–60% of daily energy should come from carbohydrates.
  5. Fibre helps bowel movement and prevents constipation.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Complex carbohydrates (rice, wheat, vegetables) are healthier than refined sugar.
  2. Carbohydrates spare protein for growth and repair.
  3. Glycogen is the storage form of glucose in liver and muscle.
  4. Fruits give fructose; milk gives lactose.

📌 Memory trick

Carbs by size: “Mono-Di-Poly” — one, two, many sugar units. Poly = starch and fibre (healthy).

60-second revision

  • Carbs = main energy source; 1 g = 4 kcal.
  • Mono-, di-, polysaccharides.
  • Sources: cereals, roots, fruits, sugar.
  • 50-60% of daily energy from carbs.
  • Fibre prevents constipation; complex carbs healthier than sugar.

Test yourself

One gram of carbohydrate gives about:

Answer: B. One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kilocalories.

Which is a polysaccharide?

Answer: C. Starch is a polysaccharide (many sugar units). Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides; sucrose is a disaccharide.

Carbohydrates should provide about what percent of daily energy?

Answer: C. About 50–60% of total daily energy should come from carbohydrates.

Fibre helps to:

Answer: B. Fibre adds bulk to stool and prevents constipation.

Which food is rich in carbohydrates?

Answer: B. Rice is a cereal rich in starch (carbohydrate).
